'Thirty replies,' Damini said, holding up her phone in the canteen. 'I asked the class group what to give Mrs Rao for the farewell.'

'Thirty? Show me,' said Kavitha.

'Look. Photo album, plants, a mug, a card everyone signs, a scarf, a video of wishes...'

'That's a lot of different things.'

'That's why I made piles. Five of them: memories, plants, useful things, something to wear, and something homemade. Memories has eleven votes if you count the album, the video and the signed card.'

'So we pick from memories?'

'First we ask everyone which pile they like, then we choose inside it.'

Kavitha grinned. 'Can I do the video?'

'You're on it.'

passage: Looking back, the farewell gift for Sen Sir was the first time I organised anything properly. I'm Vinita, and I was class rep that year. On the Monday, I posted in our class group: "Ideas for Sen Sir's farewell gift? Anything goes. Reply by Wednesday night." By Wednesday there were thirty replies, some serious, some just stickers. Omkar suggested a chess set because Sir played in the staffroom. Others wanted a plant, a photo album, a pen. I copied every idea into my notebook and grouped them: things for his hobbies, things with memories, useful things. Memories had the most, fourteen. So we made an album with a message from each of us. When Sir opened it, he went very quiet, then smiled.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel when the album was chosen over his chess set?
qa.a: Omkar might feel a small pang, but since his idea was counted and memories clearly won, he would likely still feel part of it.

Class teacher's note, 9C, Friday

This week Sharmila took on the Annual Day gift for our retiring librarian. I watched her handle it. She posted one question in the class group on Monday: "One idea each, please, by Thursday." She did not argue with anyone. By Thursday she had thirty replies. Ira helped her copy them onto chart paper in the free period, and together they grouped them: books, garden things, handmade items, experiences. Handmade had the most. Sharmila came to me with the four groups and a clear recommendation. I suggested she check the budget with the class treasurer and let the class vote between the top two groups on Monday. She looked pleased and went off to draft the poll.

qa.q: By when did Sharmila ask for ideas?
How did Sharmila seem to feel when the class teacher gave the suggestion?
qa.a: She looked pleased, suggesting she felt encouraged that her work was taken seriously.

qa.q: What could Sharmila do if the vote ended in a tie?
qa.a: She could combine the two themes, such as a handmade card with a book, or ask the librarian's closest colleague which would mean more.

qa.q: How might Ira see working on the chart paper?
qa.a: Ira likely felt useful and included, sharing the work of making sense of thirty replies.
